title: Ten question words
goal: Ask about anything — things, people, places, time, reasons, ways, amounts and choices — and answer in the right word order.
bekal: using Tagalog's ten question words with the right markers

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ang usisera
dialogs.intro: On a jeepney heading to campus. A woman sits down next to Budi and, like many Filipinos, immediately wants to know everything.

lines.speaker: Ale:
lines.id: Young man, where are you from?

lines.speaker: Ale:
lines.text: Ay! Bakit ka nandito sa Pilipinas?
lines.id: Oh! Why are you here in the Philippines?
lines.literal: oh! why you here in Philippines?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nag-aaral po ako ng Tagalog dito.
lines.literal: studying ma'am I of Tagalog here.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sa Malate po, malapit sa paaralan.
lines.id: In Malate, ma'am, near the school.
lines.literal: in Malate ma'am, near to school.

lines.speaker: Ale:
lines.id: Who do you live with there?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Mag-isa lang po ako. Pero marami akong kaibigan.
lines.id: I'm on my own, ma'am. But I have lots of friends.
lines.literal: alone just ma'am I. but many I-that friend.

lines.speaker: Ale:
lines.text: Mabuti naman. Paano mo natutunan ang Tagalog?
lines.id: Good. How did you learn Tagalog?
lines.literal: good naman. how by-you learned the Tagalog?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sa libro po at sa mga kaibigan ko. Mahirap pero masaya.
lines.id: From books, ma'am, and from my friends. Hard but fun.
lines.literal: from book ma'am and from PL friend my. hard but fun.

lines.speaker: Ale:
lines.text: Magaling ka! Sige, bababa na ako dito. Ingat ka, ha?
lines.id: You're good! Well, I'm getting off here. Take care, okay?
lines.literal: skilled you! okay, will-get-off now I here. care you, huh?

notes: **Asking strangers lots of questions is normal in the Philippines.** Age, marital status, salary, religion — anyone you've just met on a jeepney may ask. This is friendliness, not rudeness. A short answer and a smile are enough if you don't want to say much.
**Ale and Mama** are ways to address a middle-aged woman you don't know, cousins of *Aling*. For men: *Mamang* or *Manong*.
**Bakit ka nandito** — notice that *ka* attaches right after the question word. All short pronouns gather there: *Bakit ka umalis?*, *Saan mo binili?*, *Kailan ka darating?*

**Noong isang buwan** = "a month ago, last month". The pattern is *noong isang* + time unit: *noong isang linggo* (last week), *noong isang taon* (last year). For the future, the twin pattern is *sa susunod na*: *sa susunod na buwan* (next month).

**Saan asks where something happens, nasaan asks where something is.** *Saan ka nakatira?* (where do you live — where an action takes place) but *Nasaan ang bahay mo?* (where is your house). The wrong choice isn't fatal, but it's noticeable.
**Mag-isa means alone.** From *isa* (one), with the prefix *mag-*. Its cousins: *mag-isa lang* (all alone), *nag-iisa* (being alone, and a little sad about it).
**Paano asks about the way**, not about how something is going. For that, use *kumusta*. Compare: *Paano ka pumunta?* (how did you get there) versus *Kumusta ang biyahe?* (how was the trip).
**Natutunan** is the object-focus form of *matuto* (learn). You'll hear it often in questions about learning; for now, just recognize it.
**Bababa na ako dito** — a must-know sentence on a jeepney. The more common version is even shorter: *Para po!* — "Stop!", covered in unit 18.

grammars.title: Ten question words
body: Tagalog puts question words **at the start of the sentence**, like English. What needs attention is the marker that follows.
after: **Ano and alin are both "what", but not the same.** *Ano* asks without a set of options; *alin* asks you to choose from options already in front of you. *Ano ang gusto mo?* (what do you want) versus *Alin ang gusto mo?* (which one do you want).
**Gaano always pairs with an adjective starting with ka-**: *gaano katagal* (how long), *gaano kalayo* (how far), *gaano kalaki* (how big), *gaano kadalas* (how often).
After a question word, short pronouns attach right away: *Bakit **ka***, *Saan **mo***, *Ano **ang** ginagawa **mo***.

grammars.title: Answering bakit
body: "Why" questions are answered with one of two words, both equally correct — only the register differs.

head: Word
Register
Position
Example
rows: Kasi pagod ako. / Pagod kasi ako.

after: *Kaya* has two very different meanings, told apart by stress: *ka-YA* means "so, therefore", while *KA-ya* means "able" (*kaya ko* — I can).
To ask about purpose rather than cause, use *para saan* or *para kanino*: *Para kanino ito?* (who is this for).
The most honest answer Filipinos give when they don't want to explain: *Basta.* — "just because".

head: Tagalog
Meaning
Typical answer
rows: How do I get to Luneta?
How many of you are there?

blocks.text: *Saan ka galing?* uses *galing* (coming from) to ask where you've just been, not where you're from. For where you're from, use *taga-saan*. The two questions sound alike but get very different answers: *Galing akong palengke* (I've just come from the market) versus *Taga-Jakarta ako* (I'm from Jakarta).

blocks.title: Asking back politely
items: *Ikaw?* or *Kayo po?* — "and you?" The shortest, most common way to return a question.
*Ano po ulit?* — "sorry, what was that?" Use it when you didn't catch the answer and don't want the other person to feel they spoke unclearly.
*Pasensya po, hindi ko naintindihan.* — "Sorry, I didn't understand." A lifesaver worth learning whole.

blocks.text: Besides the ten question words, there are two other ways of asking that are used just as often.

*Di ba* (from *hindi ba*) is one of the most frequent expressions in Filipino conversation — used to seek agreement, to remind, or just to fill a pause. The closest English equivalent is a tag like "right?" or "isn't it?".
